title: How Personality Tests Work
summary: Josh and Chuck examine personality tests, focusing on the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI). They trace personality typing from the ancient four humors through Carl Jung's psychological types, the Briggs mother-daughter development of the MBTI during and after World War Two, and the CPP publishing and certification model. They contrast projective tests (Rorschach) with objective inventories, cover the Big Five traits, psychometrics and validity/reliability, the MMPI and its norming criticism, the Barnum/Forer effect, and criticisms of using these tests for hiring. A listener email about anxiety, TV, and relaxation closes the episode.
topics: type A and type B personality

segments.title: Opening and Myers-Briggs introduction
segments.summary: The hosts recall taking the Myers-Briggs test at work and introduce the MBTI as a widespread corporate personality inventory, with personality categorization framed as an old idea.

segments.title: Four humors and early personality types
segments.summary: The hosts describe the ancient four humors (black bile, yellow bile, phlegm, blood) and their linked temperaments: melancholic, phlegmatic, sanguine, choleric. They criticize the idea that people fit one type.

segments.title: Carl Jung and the origins of introversion
segments.summary: Carl Jung's book Psychological Types introduced the four functions of sensation, intuition, thinking, and feeling and the introvert and extrovert concepts. The hosts note Jung's relationship with Freud and the parallel movement to quantify psychology.

segments.title: Briggs mother and daughter develop the MBTI
segments.summary: Katherine Cook Briggs and her daughter Isabelle Briggs Myers developed a type indicator building on Jung, aiming to match women entering the workforce after World War Two with suitable jobs. Publishing shifted to CPP over time.

segments.title: Types of personality tests and the Big Five
segments.summary: Personality assessments are divided into projective tests (Rorschach) and objective standardized inventories. The Big Five traits are extraversion, agreeableness, openness, conscientiousness, and neuroticism, with the hosts noting a sketch of personality needs more than these traits.

segments.title: Psychometrics, validity, reliability, and faking
segments.summary: Psychometric tests use many questions and spectrum scoring to produce bell-curve distributions. Validity and reliability are key measures, and the MMPI is said to detect faking.

segments.title: How the MBTI works and its certification
segments.summary: The MBTI sorts people into sixteen types across four dichotomies: introversion/extraversion, sensing/intuition, thinking/feeling, judging/perceiving. Test questions and word pairs are described, and CPP certification costs and training are covered. The hosts discuss their own results and the type A/type B origin.
topics: type A and type B personality

segments.title: Criticisms of MBTI and corporate use
segments.summary: Critics say MBTI lacks scientific basis, that its dichotomies are spectrums forced into categories, and that its scales are entangled. Corporate use for hiring and firing is criticized, though the MBTI makers discourage it. Rorschach and the Exner comprehensive system are also covered.
topics: hiring and firing with personality tests

segments.title: MMPI and the Barnum effect
segments.summary: The MMPI was built on a control group of sane family and staff, and critics call it invasive and culturally narrow. The Barnum (Forer) effect shows people accept generic positive personality descriptions as accurate.

segments.title: Listener mail on anxiety and TV
segments.summary: A listener from the UK describes reducing anxiety by abandoning television and suggests an episode on TV's effects on society.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give social media and website contact information.
